lessons.title: Inference, Annotations, and Object Types
lessons.summary: Let TypeScript infer obvious local values; annotate public boundaries where the contract is valuable documentation.
lessons.body:
Inference, Annotations, and Object Types

Why this matters
Let TypeScript infer obvious local values; annotate public boundaries where the contract is valuable documentation. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Let TypeScript infer obvious local values; annotate public boundaries where the contract is valuable documentation.
• Object types describe required/optional properties and nested shapes.
• Structural typing means compatibility is based mainly on shape rather than class names.
• Use unknown for untrusted values until validated/narrowed; avoid any as a permanent escape hatch.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, typescript foundations stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter inference, annotations, and object types again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.

lessons.title: Unions, Literals, and Narrowing
lessons.summary: Literal unions model closed domain choices more accurately than arbitrary string.
lessons.body:
Unions, Literals, and Narrowing

Why this matters
Literal unions model closed domain choices more accurately than arbitrary string. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Literal unions model closed domain choices more accurately than arbitrary string.
• Narrowing uses checks such as typeof, in, discriminants, or user-defined predicates to prove a more specific type.
• Discriminated unions can model mutually exclusive states such as loading/success/error.
• Compiler exhaustiveness can turn new domain variants into useful compile errors.

lessons.title: Interfaces, Type Aliases, and Generics
lessons.summary: Interfaces and type aliases overlap for object modeling; choose consistency and clarity over ideology.
lessons.body:
Interfaces, Type Aliases, and Generics

Why this matters

• Interfaces and type aliases overlap for object modeling; choose consistency and clarity over ideology.

lessons.summary: Pick, Omit, Partial, Record, Awaited, and related utilities transform existing types.
lessons.body:
Utility Types and Contract Transformation

Why this matters
Pick, Omit, Partial, Record, Awaited, and related utilities transform existing types. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. Mental model
• Pick, Omit, Partial, Record, Awaited, and related utilities transform existing types.

lessons.title: TypeScript vs Runtime Validation
lessons.summary: TypeScript is erased before JavaScript executes, so external JSON can violate every declared type.
lessons.body:
TypeScript vs Runtime Validation

Why this matters
TypeScript is erased before JavaScript executes, so external JSON can violate every declared type. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• TypeScript is erased before JavaScript executes, so external JSON can violate every declared type.
• Runtime schemas such as Zod validate unknown data at trust boundaries.
• A strong pattern is parse unknown input, obtain validated typed data, then run business rules.
• Database constraints add another independent correctness layer for invariants that must survive application bugs.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, typescript foundations stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter typescript vs runtime validation again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.

Purpose

Working method
